items.title: Eventhouse support for OneLake security (Generally Available)
items.text: Sections: Lakehouse data with Eventhouse power; Object, column, and row level security; Get started. Security should be consistent wherever you query your data. With OneLake security, you can define access controls once, close to the data, and apply them across supported Microsoft Fabric engines without recreating your security rules for each experience. Today, we’re announcing the general availability of OneLake security support for Eventhouse external tables. When these external tables query data secured by OneLake security, they automatically enforce object-level, column-level, and row-level access controls. This extends the same centrally managed security model to KQL queries, helping you maintain consistent, end-to-end security and governance across analytics experiences. items.title: Find expensive queries from Capacity Metrics (Generally Available)
items.text: Sections: Follow the activity into your warehouse; Find the queries worth investigating; Make the same correlation with AI; Next steps. When warehouse capacity usage spikes, you need to quickly understand what ran, which warehouse drove the usage, and which queries require investigation. The Monitor in warehouse action in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app connects the capacity-level view directly to Warehouse Monitor. It opens the selected warehouse with the relevant time window already applied, eliminating manual correlation across monitoring experiences. Figure: Animated GIF - demonstrating how to navigate from a Capacity Metrics timepoint to Warehouse Monitor in four steps. Open Capacity Metrics: From the Compute page, select your capacity and review CU % over time. Capacity Units, or CUs, represent the compute consumption tracked for the capacity. items.title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
items.text: Sections: Write native Iceberg tables from the engines you already use; Add business context to tables and columns; Explore more in the OneLake documentation; We want your feedback!. OneLake table APIs already let Iceberg-compatible engines discover and read tables in Microsoft Fabric. Today we're taking the next step with two additions: Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) writes through the OneLake table endpoint, now available, and a new additional table metadata API, in preview, for adding descriptions and tags to tables and columns. Together, they make OneLake a place where any engine can not only read data, but also publish it, with the business context people and AI agents need to use it well. Until now, the OneLake Iceberg endpoint supported read-only metadata operations. Now, IRC-compatible clients can create native Iceberg tables, commit new snapshots, and request short-lived storage credentials through the same endpoint they already use for reads. items.title: Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake (Preview)
items.text: Sections: Introducing Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake; Getting started; Prerequisites; Configure Salesforce Data 360 shortcuts; We are excited to see what you build. A customer reports a missing delivery. The service case is in Salesforce, while the shipping and returns records are in Microsoft Fabric. Before a team can decide what to do next, it needs to connect those two views of the same customer experience. For many organizations, answering questions like this still means exporting customer data, building ingestion pipelines, and maintaining another copy for analytics. Every additional handoff adds work for data teams and another dataset to secure and reconcile. Business teams wait for a complete picture while customer decisions move ahead. Zero-copy file sharing offers a different approach by making source data available where it is needed for analysis, without first building a separate ingestion copy. The data is always current.
